title: A schoolboy watched his hot ice-cream mix freeze before the cold batch.
description:
A schoolboy watched his hot ice-cream mix freeze before the cold batch. Erasto Mpemba was in Form 3 at Magamba Secondary School. His teacher told him that was simply not possible.

"Hence many people, when they want to cool water quickly, begin by putting it in the sun." Francis Bacon and Rene Descartes both noted it too, centuries before Mpemba was born. None of that stopped it from being named after him.

A physicist who met Mpemba at his next school, tested the claim with water back in his own lab, and confirmed it. They published together in Physics Education under the title "Cool?", while Mpemba was training at the College of African Wildlife Management, not a physics department.

In 2016, two researchers finally tested it under tightly controlled conditions. Henry Burridge and Paul Linden's own conclusion: "We conclude, somewhat sadly, that there is no evidence to support meaningful observations of the Mpemba effect."

It's still taught as settled science in classrooms that have never settled it.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mpemba_effect: read in full. Establishes: Erasto Mpemba, a Tanzanian student, noticed in 1963 in Form 3 at Magamba Secondary School (Tanganyika) that a hot ice-cream mixture froze before a cold one in cookery class, and his teacher dismissed it; he later raised it with visiting physicist Denis Osborne at Mkwawa Secondary School; Osborne tested it with water at his own workplace and confirmed it; they co-published "Cool?" in Physics Education 4(3):172-175 in 1969, while Mpemba was studying at the College of African Wildlife Management; Aristotle wrote centuries earlier, "Hence many people, when they want to cool water quickly, begin by putting it in the sun"; Francis Bacon separately noted "slightly tepid water freezes more easily than that which is utterly cold"; Rene Descartes described the same pattern in his Discourse on the Method; in 2016, Henry Burridge and Paul Linden tested the time water takes to reach 0°C under tightly controlled conditions and concluded, in their own words, "We conclude, somewhat sadly, that there is no evidence to support meaningful observations of the Mpemba effect"; the article states physicists remain divided on the effect's reproducibility, precise definition and underlying mechanism.
- https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5121640: Burridge, H.C. & Linden, P.F., "Questioning the Mpemba effect: hot water does not cool more quickly than cold," Scientific Reports 6:37665 (2016), cited via the Wikipedia article's direct quotation of the paper's conclusion; title, authors, journal and year corroborated independently.
